Name: phase_locked_stokes_hysteresis
Title: Does mean phase steer polarization along a reproducible loop, or merely change its apparent quality?
Short Hypothesis: The mean-phase scan may encode a phase-locked trajectory of the exported Stokes direction, with departures from a simple closed loop arising from calibration history or drift rather than from mean phase alone. This is worth testing because the supplied scan samples mean phase across 0 to 2π, while its DOP and S1/S2/S3 are separate exported quantities; inspecting the direction trajectory can therefore test a mechanism not established by the source study’s reported controls. The supplied scan is exploratory, not independent evidence: a shuffled-phase remeasurement is needed to distinguish phase dependence from acquisition order.
Related Work: The identified source study investigates degree-of-polarization modulation under phase-distribution-spread and mean-phase controls. This proposal does not restate that result or claim rediscovery. It asks whether the mean-phase control traces a reproducible, potentially history-sensitive path in Stokes direction. The supplied corpus alone cannot establish novelty relative to the broader literature, and this direction should be treated as a focused follow-up hypothesis rather than a literature-verified gap.
Abstract: The supplied measurements contain two distinct source scans: 102 observations under a phase-spread control and 200 under a mean-phase control. We propose a focused follow-up on the latter: does sweeping mean phase steer the exported polarization direction along a reproducible path on the Stokes sphere, or can its apparent structure be explained by acquisition order, drift, or measurement noise? First, analyze the supplied mean-phase scan without pooling it with the spread scan or treating rows as independent repeats. Compare low-complexity periodic descriptions of the three exported Stokes components against order-sensitive alternatives, while separately tracking their squared norm and the exported DOP. The central prediction is conditional: if mean phase drives a stable response, randomized-order repeated sweeps should recover a phase-locked Stokes trajectory, including similar loop closure and harmonic structure; if the pattern is predominantly drift or history, it should change with sweep order or direction. A second prediction is that any relationship between DOP and Stokes-direction norm should be assessed empirically, not assumed from the exported labels. The existing measurements can motivate and constrain this test, but cannot settle it: there are no independent repeats or supplied acquisition uncertainties. This proposal converts a single source scan into a discriminating calibration experiment, separating phase-locked polarization steering from order-dependent artifacts without claiming a new finding from the supplied data.
Experiments: 1. Analyze only the 200-row mean-phase scan. Sort by mean_phase, plot S1/S2/S3 and DOP against phase, calculate r²=S1²+S2²+S3², and report extrema and descriptive summaries. Do not infer replicate-based significance or combine raw DOP values with the other scan. 2. Fit prespecified Fourier regressions to each Stokes component using sin(kφ), cos(kφ), k=1…3; compare held-out contiguous phase-block prediction error with a constant model and with a smooth nonperiodic/order trend. Report component-wise RMSE and R², and avoid treating this exploratory model comparison as confirmatory evidence. 3. Follow up with feasible repeated measurements at the same phase settings in randomized order, in both ascending and descending sweeps, with at least several sweeps per condition. Preserve exported units and record acquisition order. Compare phase-locked Fourier coefficients, loop closure (distance between endpoint directions), and within-phase variability across sweeps and orders. 4. Distinguish alternatives: stable phase dependence predicts similar trajectories across randomized, ascending, and descending sweeps; drift predicts dependence on acquisition order; hysteresis predicts direction-dependent trajectories at matched phases. Evaluate these with order-stratified prediction error and between-sweep variation, reporting uncertainty across sweeps rather than across individual rows.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The supplied mean-phase scan is a single scan with no independent repeats or acquisition-uncertainty estimates, so its apparent structure may be descriptive only. It is not established from the supplied information whether the scan’s row order represents acquisition order. The exported Stokes components are described as normalized polarization-direction components, but their norm should be measured rather than presumed to equal DOP. Fourier fits can miss sharp or nonstationary behavior and may overfit; keep harmonic order low and validate on blocked phases. The proposal depends on access to the original measurement setup for the decisive randomized and reversed sweeps. Literature novelty remains unresolved because external search was disabled.
